newsitem.title: USA: US commission sees consumer bankruptcies as challenge.
newsitem.headline: US commission sees consumer bankruptcies as challenge.

text.p: A commission reviewing the U.S. bankruptcy system sees consumer bankruptcy filings, which reached a record 1 million last year, as its biggest challenge, the commission chairman said Wednesday.
"No one wants to make it easier" for consumers to file for bankruptcy, Brady Williamson, chairman of the National Bankruptcy Review Commission, said at a seminar for congressional staffers.
The nine-member commission created by Congress in 1994 must issue its recommendations by Oct. 20. It is solely an advisory panel with no actual authority to make changes.
"The idea is to make the law fairer, more efficient for creditors and debtors alike," Williamson said.
Consumer bankruptcies are up in every district, while business bankruptcy filings are flat or down, he said.
"Consumer bankruptcy represents the commission's single biggest challenge, and its most difficult issue," he added.

The commission has so far reached agreement on about 18 issues and intends to provide a "catalog" of issues where agreement was reached and disagreements occurred, Williamson said. "I think the areas of agreement will outweigh the areas of disagreement, although there clearly will be areas of disagreement," he said.
Areas of tentative agreement by the commission include eliminating the U.S. District Court as a mandatory stop when appealing a bankruptcy court ruling, and giving bankruptcy judges life tenure.
The commission is to meet Thursday and Friday to discuss issues related to small business and consumer bankruptcies.

Bankrupty experts, also speaking at the seminar, said the rise in consumer bankruptcies needed to be examined. A former bankruptcy judgee, Roger Whelan, blamed much of the increase in consumer bankruptcy filings on credit card debt. He said the first big jump in such filings occurred in 1967, almost one year after the issuance of the first plastic credit card, when consumer bankruptcy filings doubled to 197,000 from the previous year.

Sam Gerdano, executive director at American Bankruptcy Institute, said an increase in the amount of debt consumers are taking on relative to their income has contributed to what he termed a "bankruptcy boom."
That contrasts with business bankruptcies, which have been fairly flat.
"There has not been a boom in business bankruptcies," said Christopher Beard, a lawyer who publishes a newsletter called Turnarounds and Workouts.

About 52,000 commercial bankruptcy filings last year were consistent with the prior two years, he said. "The primary reason for the number of low business bankruptcies is, of course, the economy," Beard said, adding that the economy was growing, inflation and interest rates were low and the stock market was rising.
The retail sector currently is going through "very difficult times," and the bankruptcy system is not adequately dealing with that area, Beard said.
Rapid technological changes have also had an adverse impact on some telecommunications firms unable to keep stride with the pace of the changing industry, he said.
